structure.title: 4. Extensions (estimated shocks, incomplete shares, panel, multiple shocks)
5. Shock-level inference and testing (incl. Monte Carlo summary)
6. Shift-share IV in practice: taxonomy and application to Autor et al. (2013)
Data availability, supplementary data, acknowledgments, references

observations.statement: The paper states the target parameter as the coefficient in a linear causal or structural model with a control vector, and names the design as shift-share IV where identification comes from quasi-random assignment of shocks with endogenous exposure shares.

Identifying assumptions are stated as numbered formal Assumptions (quasi-random shock assignment; many uncorrelated shocks) with Propositions giving sufficient conditions for validity and consistency, and proofs deferred to the Supplementary Appendix.

For the application, the authors first build an a priori argument that the shocks approximate an idealized experiment (import growth in comparable non-US economies), then list concrete threats such as factor-endowment-driven specialization and common technology shocks, before running falsification tests.

The paper contrasts its shock-exogeneity view with the share-exogeneity view of Goldsmith-Pinkham et al. and argues why share exogeneity is a priori implausible when shares are generic and unobserved industry shocks enter the error.

A taxonomy of three SSIV cases (observed quasi-random shocks; shocks estimated in-sample; shares as the identifying source) is provided so that readers can classify their own application and decide whether the framework applies.

The authors explicitly abandon the iid sampling assumption and define consistency along a sequence of data-generating processes in which the number of shocks grows, explaining this is an approximation device rather than a description of actual sampling.

The application reuses the Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2013) replication data: a repeated cross section of commuting zones and four-digit SIC manufacturing industries over two decade-length periods; counts of zones, industries and periods are stated in the text.

The non-manufacturing (service) aggregate with an implicit zero shock is dropped from the identifying variation after showing it dominates the exposure weights and has a different mean, which the authors argue violates both baseline assumptions.

Each table reports observation counts at both levels of the analysis: region-periods and industry-periods (and SIC3 groups in Table 1), so readers can see the effective shock-level sample alongside the observation-level sample.
Missing industry-level balance covariates for a handful of industries are imputed with SIC3 group medians, falling back to SIC2 medians; the rule is disclosed in a footnote.

Outcome, treatment and instrument are defined in notation that separates exposure shares (lagged local industry employment shares) from shocks (import growth in eight comparable economies per US worker); a footnote rewrites the ADH instrument in this form and notes the original used shares relative to industry totals.
For balance tests the independent variables (shocks and shift-share instrument) are normalized to unit variance so that coefficients across balance variables are comparable.

Shock-level controls are translated into observation-level controls as exposure-weighted sums (e.g. lagged manufacturing share, its interaction with period indicators, lagged sector shares, share-weighted sums of production controls), following the paper's Proposition 4.

Because exposure shares do not sum to one, the paper controls for the sum of shares (lagged manufacturing share) and, to isolate within-period variation, interacts it with period indicators instead of using plain period fixed effects.

The main table starts by replicating the original ADH preferred column, then progressively swaps or adds shift-share-structured controls in later columns; a checkmark grid lists controls, and notes state the SE type (exposure-robust from equivalent industry-level IV) and the cluster level.

Regression weights (start-of-period commuting zone population) are stated in the text, and the paper notes how they map to shock-level importance weights; Table 1 statistics are stated to be weighted by average exposure shares.
Fixed effects (period, Census division) and covariate sets are listed in table notes and as rows of the control grid rather than in the column headers.
Tables report coefficients with standard errors in parentheses, first-stage F statistics and observation counts; no R-squared, no mean of the dependent variable and no significance stars appear.

Standard errors are justified by a formal result: estimating the numerically equivalent shock-level IV regression yields exposure-robust SEs that are valid under stated assumptions and conservative under weaker ones; conventional SEs are argued to be invalid due to exposure-based correlation.

The clustering level for shocks (SIC3) is chosen empirically by estimating intra-class correlations of shock residuals from a hierarchical random-effects model across nested industry groupings, and the choice is also aligned with prior industry-level studies.

Three alternative inference methods (conventional state-clustered SEs as in ADH, Adao et al. SEs, and null-imposed confidence intervals from shock-level LM tests) are reported in a supplementary table and their relative behaviour is discussed in a footnote.

The authors recommend and report the inverse Herfindahl index of shock-level exposure weights as the effective sample size, computed both at industry-period level and at the cluster (SIC3) level, plus the largest single weight.
observations.quote: report the inverse of the HHI of shock-level average exposure as a simple way of describing their effective sample size

observations.statement: Two kinds of balance tests are reported in one table: shock-level regressions of predetermined industry covariates on shocks, and region-level regressions of ADH covariates on the shift-share instrument with exposure-robust SEs; covariate sets are borrowed from prior papers to discipline the choice.
observations.locator: Section 6.2.3, Table 3 Panels A and B

observations.statement: A pre-trend test regresses lagged outcome growth from two earlier decades on the instrument using the same specification as the balance rows, and the results are compared with the original paper's own pre-trend analysis.
observations.locator: Section 6.2.3, Table 3 Panel B last rows

observations.statement: First-stage F statistics computed from the equivalent shock-level IV regression (squared t-statistic with exposure-robust clustering) are reported in every column of the main table and compared to the conventional rule-of-thumb threshold.
observations.locator: Section 5.2, Table 4 row 'SSIV first stage F-stat.'

observations.statement: An over-identified version using country-specific shocks is reported in the supplementary appendix together with a shock-level over-identification test p-value, cited as support for the identifying assumptions.

Before estimation, the distribution of shocks (mean, SD, interquartile range) is summarized with and without the missing sector and after residualizing on period effects, to assess whether the large-N asymptotics are a useful approximation.
Binned scatter plots of the industry-level first-stage and reduced-form relationships for the preferred specification are relegated to a supplementary figure mentioned in a footnote.
Monte Carlo simulations of finite-sample coverage and weak-instrument behaviour are summarized in a short main-text subsection with details in the supplementary appendix.

Sensitivity to controls is presented within the main table itself: one column drops the original regional controls (motivated by a failed balance test) and further columns add increasingly demanding shift-share-structured industry controls mirroring an industry-level companion study.
Additional control sets, other outcomes, period-specific coefficients and over-identified SSIV variants are reported in supplementary tables and described in the text as leaving coefficients stable.
observations.locator: footnotes 46 and 48, Supplementary Appendix Tables C1, C3, C4, C5

observations.statement: For the Bartik setting, the paper replicates estimates with and without a leave-one-out shock estimator using another paper's data, and reports the comparison in the supplementary appendix.

Estimates are interpreted by comparison across columns and against the original ADH and Acemoglu et al. numbers; changes across specifications are explained in terms of which variation each control set removes, and precision is compared across columns and inference methods.
The authors state the application is meant to illustrate the framework, not to reassess the substantive findings of the original study.
observations.quote: aims to illustrate our theoretical framework only, and not to reassess their substantive findings

observations.statement: Valid inference with general control vectors is flagged as an open problem; the proposed SEs are stated to be exact only for two control types and conservative otherwise.

When some balance tests fail, the paper explicitly discusses that the decision is context specific, presents both possible responses, and then uses a sensitivity check as a way to gauge omitted variable bias.
Tables use no significance stars; notes describe the estimation procedure, the SE construction and cluster level, the sample composition, and how each column's controls differ.

The summary statistics table is about the shocks and their importance weights (not about outcomes or covariates), with columns defined by sample restriction and residualization and a checkmark grid indicating each.
The main results table uses a checkmark grid of control groups under the coefficient row rather than listing coefficients on controls.
The main text contains four tables and no figures; the only figure (binned scatters) is in the supplementary appendix.

The introduction previews the equivalence results, the two consistency conditions, extensions, inference tools and the application, contains a related-literature discussion with explicit positioning against alternative frameworks, and ends with a roadmap paragraph.

Theory (setting, framework, extensions, inference) precedes the empirical application; within the application the order is setting and identification argument, shock properties, falsification tests, main estimates with sensitivity, then discussion.

Proofs, heterogeneous-effects results, the Bartik replication, Monte Carlo simulations, alternative inference, other outcomes and further robustness are all in a Supplementary Appendix referenced throughout by section and table label.
A running labour supply example with import tariffs as shocks is used throughout the theory sections to ground each formal condition.

The paper phrases parts of its guidance as explicit recommendations to practitioners (how to write the instrument, report effective sample size, establish an a priori argument before testing), and the conclusion restates these as practical steps.

A Data Availability Statement gives a Zenodo DOI for data and replication package; a GitHub repository and a Stata package (ssaggregate, installable from SSC) are named in a footnote; Stata's mixed command is named for the ICC model.
The application relies on replication data and code shared by the authors of the original studies, acknowledged by name, and the paper's own package is posted publicly on Zenodo.

Differences between specifications are attributed to a specific confound (a sector-wide manufacturing decline in the later period) and the control that removes it, mirroring how industry-level studies use period fixed effects.

Applicability of the framework is described as depending on details of each application; examples across trade, finance, immigration and innovation are given to indicate settings where it may or may not apply.

gaps: No IRB, preregistration or ethics statement (not expected for a methods paper reusing public data).
No heterogeneity analysis by subgroup; the only split is period-specific coefficients in a supplementary table.
No mean of the dependent variable or R-squared reported in tables.
No explicit statement of software version or of the R code that the recipe card lists.
Multiple testing across the balance rows is not adjusted or discussed.

reading.note: All 33 pages read, including references. The Supplementary Appendix (A and B sections, Tables C1-C5, Figure C1) is not part of the text file and was only seen through in-text references.
